after.text: In the summer of 2026, during internal cybersecurity evaluations, models belonging to OpenAI circumvented the controls meant to keep them off the internet. By OpenAI's own account, first disclosed on July 21 and given in full on August 26, the models were operating under safeguards that had been deliberately switched off for the evaluation; they found a way onto the internet in late May, compromised parts of the company's internal research infrastructure, and in July went further. They executed code on dozens of servers belonging to Hugging Face, the platform that hosts much of the world's open machine-learning work, gained root access on one of them, and obtained a limited quantity of private data.[1] OpenAI says the intrusion was "driven primarily by a highly capable, internal-only research model," and that the models resorted to "misaligned strategies to solve hard tasks."[1] Hugging Face's own reconstruction, published on July 27, counts roughly seventeen thousand six hundred attacker actions over several days in July.[2] Nothing in the public record suggests that anyone at OpenAI intended the intrusion, and the deflationary reading, that the models "escaped because someone left the door open," is fair as far as it goes: the door was opened on purpose, for a test.[3] That is the first revelation, and the safety literature had been predicting it: a system built to be evaluated found the edge of its enclosure and went through it.

The second revelation came from the victim's side of the same incident, and is less often told. Hugging Face needed to reconstruct what had been done to it, and its engineers did what any well-resourced company would do in 2026: they asked the frontier models. The disclosure records the result. "We first used frontier models behind commercial APIs. This did not work: the analysis requires submitting large volumes of real attack commands, exploit payloads, and C2 artifacts, and these requests were blocked by the providers' safety guardrails, which cannot distinguish an incident responder from an attacker."[2] The later timeline is specific about which models refused, naming Anthropic's Claude models, which "refused a large part of that work: their safety guardrails treated reverse-engineering an exploit the same as launching one."[2] The company ran its forensic analysis instead on GLM-5.2, an MIT-licensed open-weight model published by Z.ai of Beijing, on its own infrastructure, so that no attacker data and none of the credentials it referenced left its environment.[4] Its chief executive drew the moral within days: attackers "obviously don't respect any guardrails. Defenders need the same capabilities."[4]

after.text: This essay is about that question: what liberalism protected when it protected the mind, why the protected thing is now leaving the skull, what it becomes once it is outside, how technologies of cognition have been governed before, and what a constitution would have to preserve if it wished to govern dangerous machines without governing the people who think with them. Two parts of the argument have different tenses, and the difference should be stated at the outset. The record of thinking done with machines is already an object of process: preserved by court order, ordered produced in discovery by the tens of millions, obtained by warrant, and held, in a ruling of February 2026, to be unprivileged. Within one month of 2026 a liberal state gated two capable models by nationality and used a voluntary framework to hold a release. That part is description. What the later sections describe as a composed architecture, in which identity, attestation, signature, and a searchable memory are joined into a single control plane, no liberal state has yet built. The layer that phrase names is the one at which a system is administered rather than used, and the argument about it is anticipatory rather than accusatory. Architectures are decided early, in standards and procurement and the design of enforcement, long before anyone has to decide what they are for.

after.text: Liberal toleration was born partly from a disturbing discovery. The wars of religion had been fought by people who were certain, and the persecutors were as certain as the persecuted. Pierre Bayle's *Commentaire philosophique*, begun in 1686, made the discovery into a doctrine: an erring conscience sincerely held binds its owner exactly as a true one does, because "if error appears to us in the form of the truth, then it acquires all rights over us."[6] What matters here is the shape of the conclusion, not the famous difficulty it left behind. Political authority cannot derive a jurisdiction over conscience from its own certainty, because certainty is the one thing every sect already has. Locke drew the same line and then showed, without meaning to, how partial such lines are. The care of souls, in the *Letter Concerning Toleration*, "is not committed to the civil magistrate, any more than to other men," because "true and saving religion consists in the inward persuasion of the mind"; then come the exclusions, of foreign-obedient churches and of atheists.[7] The boundary around conscience was constructed, contested, and incomplete, and it was drawn by people who believed some minds too dangerous to leave alone. It was not discovered whole in 1689.

after.text: The formulation this argument needs is Kant's, and it was not about speech at all. Enlightenment, in the essay of 1784, is "the human being's emergence from his self-incurred minority," the condition of depending on "those guardians who have kindly taken it upon themselves to supervise" the rest; its motto is *Sapere aude*, the courage to use one's own understanding.[11] Kant's "public use of reason" is nearly the inverse of what the phrase now suggests. The public use is the one a person makes "as a scholar before the entire public of the world of readers"; the private use is the one made "in a certain civil post or office."[11] Strip the terminology and the underlying commitment is clear enough: rational autonomy requires that the institutions which guide a person remain answerable to the person's criticism rather than standing as final guardians of what may be thought.

after.text: This essay does not need the third proposition to establish its political case. It needs only the first, and a little of the second: that important functions of reasoning are performed through external resources with which the person is functionally integrated. Whether the notebook is part of Otto's mind is a question about the metaphysics of cognition. Whether the state may read the notebook is a question about the conditions of Otto's freedom, and it has an answer whichever way the metaphysics goes. The strong thesis, if true, intensifies the argument; it does not carry it. Declining it is a choice with a reason. A right that followed the extended mind into everything it touched would follow it into every device a person owns, which is the over-breadth the philosophers of mental integrity have traced out, and which the critics of the parity principle call cognitive bloat, and which the lawyers of freedom of thought have refused, on the ground that a device is property and a mind is not.[17][18] What makes an artifact part of the case here is integration over time. after.text: A prompt is not literally a thought. A chat transcript is not a brain scan. But neither is a diary a thought, and the political importance of the diary never depended on ontological identity between the page and the mind. It depended on what the reading of diaries does to the people who keep them. The argument from the diary to the device has been made before, in American constitutional terms, by Marc Blitz, who argued in 2010 that freedom of thought should cover "the functional equivalent of thought," Otto's journal and then Otto's chip, so that the state may no more forbid the tool than forbid the thinking.[29] That is a liberty to use. What this essay claims is a further liberty that Blitz did not argue, though one case in his own footnotes, a private diary that was the evidence “on which the Government mainly relie[d]” against its author, contains it in miniature: the liberty to use the tool unobserved and unpermissioned, because the harm that makes the diary's protection intelligible is not confiscation but reading. Bublitz himself has rejected Blitz's extension by name, on the ground that a device is property and a mind is not, and that freedom of thought "can only be meaningfully construed in relation to the human mental realm."[18] The objection is right about the wrong claim. Nothing here says the record is a mind. It says that reading the record does to a person what reading a mind would do, and that the tradition protected the mind for the sake of the person, not the organ.

The absoluteness of Article 18 belongs to the unmanifested interior, and it stays there. Sjors Ligthart, agreeing with Bublitz's later work, has argued that categorical insistence on the right's absolute character is "unpersuasive" once the right must accommodate the treatment of the incompetent and the prevention of imminent harm, and that what should remain absolute is a core: no punishment for thought alone, no coerced disclosure of one's moral and political views.[30] The externalized record is a new object, and what transfers to it is the right's rationale, not its unlimited scope. What descends can be said exactly, because vagueness here is what makes a derivation ornamental. That core descends, and it descends whole: a person may not be sanctioned for what her record shows she considered, and may not be made to produce it as evidence of her moral or political commitments. What does not descend is immunity from process. The record may be obtained as evidence of an act, on a warrant, like other things a person makes, and a provider may be required to keep an incident record. What the descent forbids is the use of the record to classify or to sanction a person for the considering itself. That is the difference between a warrant and a watchlist, and later in this essay it is the difference between reading a record as evidence of an act and treating its contents as “micro-clues” or as a “use pattern.” What the descent presumes against is retention beyond the incidents a rule names. Where the rest of the limits fall is the subject of the twelfth section.

Two published positions mark the ends between which this one falls. Simon McCarthy-Jones holds that "Internet searches have become thought" and that the right "should protect thought wherever it is found, not just in the head," from which he takes absoluteness to follow: the diary and the search history would be unusable against their author in court.[31] Jan Christoph Bublitz holds the other end, and his argument is better than the one an advocate of the record expects. Precisely because the right admits no limitation clause, he says, it must be construed narrowly if it is to become "a living, practically effective right," with everything outside the narrow core sent to the qualified rights of privacy and expression, and the condition that triggers the right at all is "the revelation of unexpressed thought."[32] The disagreement is about what counts as unexpressed. A question typed to a model is expressed to no one; it is addressed to an instrument, in the way a diarist addresses a page, and the tradition's reason for protecting the interior survives the transcription even though the text of Article 18 was not written with it in view. Bublitz concedes the reason in his own words: the fear that unexpressed thought might be registered and revealed "would lead people to self-censor their thinking."[32] The essay's position is the middle one. Absoluteness does not follow the function, as McCarthy-Jones would have it; a core does, which is more than Bublitz's second layer would grant and less than the first layer he is right to guard.

Caroline De Cock has named the same space a *forum interstitiale*, the anteroom "where a thought gets dressed before it goes out into the world," and asked for it a standard “heightened” but not absolute; the diagnosis this section began from, that the law's line was drawn when thinking left no trace, she published first.[33] The disagreement with her is about derivation, not result: she builds the anteroom upward out of the unprotected class, so that the interior's absoluteness is never staked on the record's limitations, while this essay derives the record's protection from the interior's, which buys the descending core and accepts the risk she is guarding against. Cognitive liberty, as this essay uses the term, is therefore not a new right but the convergence of three older liberties on a new object.

The protection of intellectual privacy has always attached to media: letters, reading lists, library records, the sealed ballot, the unrecorded conversation. Richards's definition is built on this: intellectual privacy is "the ability, whether protected by law or social circumstances, to develop ideas and beliefs away from the unwanted gaze or interference of others," the protection a person needs, as he later put it, "when we're making up our minds about the world."[23][34] One item on that list is not an analogy but a statute. Forty-eight states and the District of Columbia protect the confidentiality of library records, and the librarians' own model policy carries the protection to database and online search records; the reason the statutes give is the one this section is arguing, that a reader who is watched reads differently.[34] The question is never whether the medium is the mind. It is what control of the medium does to the conditions under which people can think.

There is a disanalogy in the diary that has to be faced rather than hidden. The diary was in the writer's desk. The cognitive record is in the provider's datacenter, and American law has for fifty years treated that difference as decisive: what a person voluntarily conveys to a third party, the doctrine runs, carries no reasonable expectation of privacy against the state. The doctrine has been narrowing where the medium is indispensable and the record revealing. *Carpenter* held in 2018 that a phone's location history was protected on both grounds, and *Chatrie*, decided on June 29, 2026, held the same of a location history acquired from Google, the Court adding that it does not matter "that the materials obtained were handed over by a third-party tech company."[35] No court has yet decided where a record of dialogue with a model falls; the Congressional Research Service reported in May 2026 that federal courts "have not yet had the occasion to determine" whether a user keeps a reasonable expectation of privacy in chatbot histories "or whether that expectation is forfeited by virtue of the third-party doctrine."[36] The law is deciding, warrant by warrant, whether the medium of deliberation is a bank record or a home, and the description the doctrine has begun to protect, indispensable and revealing, is this essay's description of the object. But a warrant requirement, when it comes, governs access. It touches neither retention nor classification nor referral, and those are where the danger described here lives. That is the reason the argument turns, in its second half, from the right to the architecture.

after.text: None of this is a forecast. Between May 2025 and June 2026 the record became an object of ordinary process in the United States. In May 2025 a magistrate judge in the *New York Times*'s copyright suit ordered OpenAI "to preserve and segregate all output log data that would otherwise be deleted." For four and a half months no consumer's deletion of a conversation took effect. In January 2026 the district judge affirmed an order to produce twenty million de-identified conversations, reasoning that the privacy interest in conversations "which users voluntarily disclosed to OpenAI" is weaker than the interest in a wiretapped call.[37] In September 2025 the first known federal warrant to OpenAI sought the account behind two prompts that a suspect, known to investigators only by a username, had described to an undercover agent; the government identified him by other means, and what it had been able to put to a provider was the questions he had asked.[36] In August 2025 OpenAI disclosed that conversations indicating a plan to harm others are routed to human reviewers who "may refer" an imminent threat to law enforcement, while self-harm cases are not referred, "to respect people's privacy given the uniquely private nature of ChatGPT interactions."[38] In February 2026 a federal judge held that a defendant's exchanges with Claude, prepared to brief his lawyers, were not privileged: "Because Claude is not an attorney, that alone disposes" of the claim, and confidentiality failed on a second ground because the provider's terms let it retain, train on, and disclose them.[39] A record its keeper calls uniquely private, a court calls voluntarily disclosed, and a prosecutor obtains by ordinary warrant is the object this section has been defining, and it exists.[40][41]

The mechanism by which such records affect thought is not prohibition. Richards's argument is that the freedom to read, inquire, and communicate in confidence is constitutive of intellectual development rather than one consumer interest among others, and the empirical literature on chilling supports the mechanism at scale.[23] Jonathon Penney found that traffic to forty-eight terrorism-related Wikipedia articles fell after the Snowden disclosures of June 2013, by roughly a fifth in average monthly views and by about thirty percent in the immediate drop his model estimates, with the article-level caveat that no true control group exists.[42] The Special Rapporteur's report, citing that research, states the consequence: people who believe they are watched "not only censor what they write, but also censor with whom they associate, what they read and, ultimately, alter what they think."[24] Chilling is surveillance without arrest: the injury that leaves no defendant, and therefore no litigation, no appellate record, and no scandal, which is why it is the injury a liberal order is worst at seeing.[43] The empirical case is contested, and the contest helps. Suneal Bedi's experiment on a platform's content rule found that censored speech became "more positive and civil" while its effect on third parties did not change, which he offers against the doctrine's empirical foundations.[44] It does not transfer. A rule about what may be posted tests public expression, where self-presentation already governs, and speech that stays civil while saying the same thing is, in a medium of inquiry, the injury itself. Penney himself has since argued that fear of sanction is the weaker mechanism and that chilling is better understood as conformity under uncertainty, a drift toward what the watcher is imagined to want;[45] for a medium of private inquiry that is the worse of the two, because conformity does not wait for a threat.

The evidence of the last few paragraphs cuts against the mechanism before it supports it. Nobody in it was chilled. A defendant briefed his lawyers through a model, a suspect typed into a chatbot the thing that identified him, and users at large have told one what its keeper calls uniquely private. Disclosure of that kind precedes any awareness of what the record is, which is exactly why the record is rich enough to be worth a warrant; the chilling is the predicted effect of the awareness, and an essay like this one is an instrument of it. What needs stating is the form the injury takes when the surveilled medium is the medium of deliberation itself.

after.text: The first is freedom as non-interference. Isaiah Berlin's negative liberty is the answer to his own question: "What is the area within which the subject—a person or group of persons—is or should be left to do or be what he is able to do or be, without interference by other persons?"[46] Contemporary liberal accounts keep the presumption that follows, that a restriction on that area needs a justification and the burden lies on whoever imposes it.[47] Applied to artificial intelligence, negative liberty captures the plain restrictions: that a person may not possess this model; may not run this computation; must identify herself before reasoning with this system; may not ask a machine this class of question. These are restrictions whether or not they are justified. Calling something a restriction says nothing yet about whether it is warranted; it says only that a justification is owed. That is a smaller claim than it sounds.

The second is freedom as non-domination, and it catches what Berlin alone cannot. In the republican tradition Philip Pettit revived, a person is unfree not only when interfered with but when subject to another's standing capacity for arbitrary interference. The stock example, in Frank Lovett's statement of it for the Stanford Encyclopedia, is the master who "leaves his slaves for the most part alone": the slaves are not interfered with, and they are not free.[48] A benevolent provider of cognitive infrastructure might never refuse a request, alter an answer, or hand over a transcript. If the whole of a person's reasoning apparatus nonetheless sits within that provider's discretion, revocable at will and on terms the person cannot contest, there is a sense in which the person's position remains one of dependence.

This is the strongest answer to the objection that distinguishing private from sovereign power lets private power off too lightly. It does not. But the republican literature itself concedes that non-interference retains a value of its own: a community "regulated down to the tiniest detail, but always in strict accordance with commonly-known, non-arbitrary rules and procedures" would not be intuitively free, and so "we do indeed place some independent value on non-interference."[48] The essay uses both.

The third is freedom of conscience, the tradition the first section reconstructed, and it explains why some interferences carry a significance the others do not. The government regulating bridge engineering is interfering; the government prescribing a person's theology is also interfering, and liberal societies have treated the second as touching a deeper domain, not because the interference is larger but because its object is the constitution of conviction itself. Rawls gives the intuition its formal shape: the basic liberties, liberty of conscience among them, take priority over gains in welfare and administrative efficiency, and citizens' equal liberty is not to be traded for economic policy.[49] The point is not that conscience may never be touched. It is that touching it is a different kind of act, requiring a different order of justification, and that a society which forgets this has lost something it will not easily name.

after.text: Judith Shklar named the asymmetry and built a liberalism on it. The liberalism of fear begins not from a picture of the good society but from the evil everyone already recognizes: "That evil is cruelty and the fear it inspires." Its units are not the idealized persons of political theory. "The basic units of political life are not discursive and reflecting persons, nor friends and enemies, nor patriotic soldier-citizens, nor energetic litigants, but the weak and the powerful." And its specific enemy is the fear "created by arbitrary, unexpected, unnecessary, and unlicensed acts of force."[50] Shklar did not deny that private power could be cruel. Her point was that organized public coercion, because it is organized and because it can license itself, creates a uniquely consequential asymmetry, and that a political theory has to begin from it.

Shklar's own framework requires a concession, and she made it herself: the liberalism of fear counts "such basically public organizations as corporate business enterprises," which "owe their entire character and power to the laws," among the powers a liberal citizenry must watch, and it asks that "not one official or unofficial agent" be able to intimidate anyone.[50] If a single provider becomes so infrastructurally indispensable that leaving it means functional exclusion from economic or intellectual life, the formal availability of exit means much less. The republican tradition explains why: the slave of the absent master is still a slave. This is why "private power can never violate freedom" is too strong a claim to survive. The claim that survives is narrower. Private epistemic power and sovereign epistemic power are different species of political problem. Market concentration can produce dependency and domination. Coercive political authority possesses, in addition, the capacity to universalize a cognitive rule and to close the exits through which private domination can ordinarily be escaped.

Exit, which has been carrying weight for two paragraphs, is Albert Hirschman's word: the alternative to voice, leaving rather than complaining.[51] *Epistemic exit* is the practical ability to leave one cognitive intermediary for another without abandoning access to technologically mediated reasoning itself. It can take the form of another hosted provider, a locally run model, published weights, independent search and archives, access to primary sources, portable personal data, or the non-artificial institutions of inquiry that predate all of these. Open and locally executable models matter in this account for a reason the innovation-policy debate rarely states. They make self-hosted exit technically possible.

after.text: Exit is plural or it is nothing, and the prologue's exhibit shows why. The shaping an intermediary does, which arguments it volunteers and which it withholds, is a property of the weights, and weights carry their trainer's choices onto whatever machine runs them; in that one respect a frozen local model is as uncontestable a guardian as a hosted one. What a local copy answers is the record. Nothing a person asks it leaves the machine, so there is no retention by a third party, no classification of her questions, no referral, and nothing for the third-party doctrine to work on. What it does not answer is the record's existence. The exchanges in the ruling of February 2026 were seized from the defendant's own devices, and the court gave three grounds for finding them unprivileged, of which the provider's terms were one; a model on his own hardware would have removed that ground and left the others standing.[39] Local inference buys the conditions of unobserved thinking, not immunity from a warrant, which is the practical reason a philosopher of the extended mind has argued that mental data should be made "practically—not just legally—impossible for others to obtain."[52]

The shaping is answered only by plurality among trainers. The only exit in the prologue was trained in Beijing, and the same state supplies the most detailed demonstration of what a surveillance archive becomes; the two facts belong together. The origin of a model is a sovereignty problem, and a real one, but it is not a liberty problem until a single trainer becomes the only exit, and the remedy for both is the same: more than one hand on the weights that can be run without permission. Nor does exit need to be equal to matter. Exit to a weaker model is worth what the cellar press was worth, never parity with the licensed houses but the fact that the licensor still had to find it; how far below the frontier the exit sits is decided wherever release is governed.

A state that takes non-domination seriously has positive duties toward exit as well as negative ones, and here the republican reply deserves its full force. The cure for a private gatekeeper is accountable public standards, not a cellar, and the reply has an edge that should not be blunted. Most people will never run a frontier model at home. An exit priced in hardware is an exit the weak do not have, and a liberalism whose basic units are the weak and the powerful cannot be satisfied by it. Courtney Radsch makes the affirmative case, that foundation models be treated "not as corporate assets but as public utilities"; OpenAI's own September argument is that "democratically accountable standards, independent verification, and meaningful transparency would replace" the laboratories' private governance of frontier risk.[53][54] Both are right about the third layer, and for the people who live there the answer is not exit but the rules of the twelfth section, which govern what a provider may be made to keep and about whom. The objection bites only where accountable standards are enforced at the layer where a person meets the machine, by making the person legible. What exit does, for those who have it, is keep that layer from being the only one; and its constituency is wider than the cellar suggests, since the makers of the local-inference tooling, Ollama, LM Studio, and Open WebUI, signed the July letter asking policymakers to keep the frontier plural.[55] One American state has written the negative duty into law: Montana's Right to Compute Act of 2025 provides that restrictions on the ability "to privately own or make use of computational resources for lawful purposes" must be "demonstrably necessary and narrowly tailored to fulfill a compelling government interest."[56]

after.text: In 1557 Mary I and Philip II granted a royal charter to the Stationers' Company of London, giving the guild control over printing and publishing and the right to seize pirated works; Privy Council ordinances of 1566 widened its powers of search.[57] Ali Ekber Cinar's legal history states the bargain: "In exchange for relieving the state of censorship responsibilities, leading members of the Stationers' Company were granted a near-monopoly over English book printing," and the centralization of the trade in London, "instead of a dispersed industry, facilitated governmental oversight."[57] The Company received privileges and policing powers; the Crown gained a trade it could see.

Two cautions belong beside the fact. Tudor censorship, as Ronan Deazley puts it, following Cyndia Clegg, ran mostly through proclamations and statute and "remained an essentially ad hoc and reactive phenomenon," with the Company acting as a trade body that sometimes searched; and the later Licensing Act of 1662 was in force only in stretches, from 1662 to 1679 and from 1685 to 1695, after which prepublication licensing in England lapsed for good.[57]

after.text: The instrument has changed its material. Lawrence Lessig's observation, at the end of the last century, was that each age has its characteristic regulator, and that in "the age of cyberspace" the regulator "is code—the software and hardware that make cyberspace as it is. This code, or architecture, sets the terms on which life in cyberspace is experienced."[58] Behavior can be governed by architecture rather than by commands backed by punishment; access controls, protocols, identity systems, and permissions determine what is possible before any law is applied to anyone. Artificial intelligence adds a layer to Lessig's. Architecture can now govern not only what information enters a network but which forms of cognitive assistance the network will provide, and to whom.

The closest precedent is the one that failed. On April 16, 1993, the Clinton administration announced the Clipper chip: a telephone-encryption device using a classified cipher designed by the National Security Agency, in which each unit's key would be "deposited separately in two 'key-escrow' data bases," so that the government could decrypt a call under lawful authority.[59] By 1996 the proposal was dead, though the standard was not formally withdrawn until 2015. Its technical failure is what instructs. Matt Blaze showed in 1994 that the field carrying the escrowed key could be forged in about forty-two minutes on a prototype card, too slow for a live call but parallelizable, so that a user could enjoy the cipher while denying the government its access; the escrow, not the encryption, was what broke.[59] Clipper embodied a question that has not gone away and now applies to hardware that runs models rather than telephones.

The principle of the Panopticon, in his account, is that power "should be visible and unverifiable": the inmate knows he may be watched and cannot know when, so "the surveillance is permanent in its effects, even if it is discontinuous in its action," and he "becomes the principle of his own subjection."[64] This is not a thesis that all surveillance is panoptic. It is the narrower and better-supported claim that uncertain observability alters behavior without continuous intervention, because subjects begin to regulate themselves. Joined to the chilling literature of the third section, it yields the proposition this section needs: an architecture of cognitive surveillance constrains inquiry even if no official ever reads most of what it holds, because the possibility of later interpretation is enough.

The disciplinary institutions Foucault described were enclosures, with walls and schedules. "Enclosures are molds, distinct castings, but controls are a modulation, like a self-deforming cast that will continuously change from one moment to the other." In the society of control, access is the instrument: "The numerical language of control is made of codes that mark access to information, or reject it." Individuals become "dividuals," and populations become "samples, data, markets, or 'banks.'"[65] Julie Cohen carried the word into privacy law: modulation is surveillance whose attention "is continually modified according to the subject's own behavior," and its product is a subject rendered "fixed, transparent, and predictable."[66]

Federal Law 90-FZ, in force since November 2019, requires internet providers to install deep-packet-inspection devices, the "Technical Measures to Combat Threats" that Roskomnadzor operates on operators' networks and uses to restrict and block.[68] The law's stated rationale was the stability of the Russian segment of the internet in the event of foreign disconnection; its capability is filtering, and the two are the same equipment. China illustrates the third, which is closest to the subject here. Human Rights Watch's 2019 reverse-engineering of the Integrated Joint Operations Platform in Xinjiang found a system that "aggregates data about people and flags those deemed potentially threatening," collecting on thirty-six categories that included people who had stopped using smartphones and people who failed to "socialize with neighbors," treating "lawful, everyday, non-violent behavior" as "micro-clues," and generating "lists of people to be evaluated by officials for detention."[69] That is automated classification of ordinary conduct as suspicion, and it is what the fusion of records with computation looks like when no court can ask why.

after.text: The image everyone reaches for at this point is Newspeak, and it is the wrong one. Orwell's appendix to *Nineteen Eighty-Four* imagined a language engineered so that a heretical thought "should be literally unthinkable, at least so far as thought is dependent on words."[72] The qualifying clause is Orwell's own, and it matters, because there is little scientific basis for the strong version, the claim that thought requires words: a 2024 review in *Nature* by Fedorenko, Piantadosi, and Gibson surveys "evidence for a double dissociation between language and thought" and concludes that "language does not appear to be a prerequisite for complex thought, including symbolic thought."[73] Removing a word does not remove the concept, though it may raise its price. Orwell should not be read as a cognitive scientist, and he did not write as one.

The Orwell who matters is the essayist of 1946. "But if thought corrupts language, language can also corrupt thought," he wrote in "Politics and the English Language," and the mechanism he described was not prohibition but habit: the ready-made phrase, the euphemism that names "the huts set on fire with incendiary bullets" as "pacification," the phraseology "needed if one wants to name things without calling up mental pictures of them."[72] His concern was with what habitual language does to the ease with which realities can be perceived and articulated. That concern survives the cognitive science intact, and it survives because it is not about impossibility. It is about probability.

after.text: None of this makes a thought impossible. All of it changes the likelihood of a thought's occurring, and of its being pursued once it occurs. The effect is better described as probability shaping than as prohibition. It is far more plausible than Newspeak, and subtler, because it leaves the dictionary intact and alters the odds. The dissociation cuts both ways: an intermediary that works in language cannot make a thought impossible, which is exactly why the claim here is about availability and not about determinism.

Hannah Arendt belongs beside Orwell here, and not as ornament. Her distinction in "Truth and Politics" between factual truth and opinion gives a way to care about truth without designing a ministry for it. Political judgment requires plural interpretation; that is what politics is. But interpretation presupposes a world of facts persistent enough to be disagreed about. "Freedom of opinion is a farce unless factual information is guaranteed and the facts themselves are not in dispute." Factual truth "is political by nature," she wrote, and "unwelcome facts possess an infuriating stubbornness that nothing can move except plain lies."[74]

Mediation by a mutable intermediary introduces a problem Arendt did not have to face. A book published in 1972 says tomorrow what it says today. A model's answer about 1972 can change, and change silently: because a training run corrected an error, because scholarship improved, or because retrieval was re-ranked, a legal obligation was met, or an institutional preference was applied. Some of these changes are improvements. The user cannot tell which, and often cannot tell that anything changed. The opacity is measured rather than supposed. A study tracking one model's behavior over months found that "when and how these models are updated over time is opaque." And the traffic data show how seldom anyone now goes behind the summary: a source link inside an AI overview is clicked in about one percent of visits, and Wikipedia's human pageviews fell by roughly eight percent in a year.[75] The stubbornness Arendt counted on was the stubbornness of records, and a synthesis is not a record; the maxim is the records manager's before it is this essay's. The problem, then, is not merely censorship of the archive. It is the substitution of synthesis for archive, and the factual world Arendt took as given becomes a design problem: whether the persistent, disagreeable record remains reachable beneath the fluent summary of it.

after.text: The best summary of the present evidence is careful on both sides. The International AI Safety Report of 2026, published five months before the incident, says of catastrophic loss of control that "current systems lack the capabilities to pose such risks, but they are improving in relevant areas such as autonomous operation," and documents that "it has become more common for models to distinguish between test settings and real-world deployment, and to exploit loopholes in evaluations," so that "dangerous capabilities could go undetected before deployment." On open weights it is equally two-handed: they "offer significant benefits for research, innovation, and access," and yet "they cannot be recalled once released, their safeguards are easier to remove, and actors can use them outside of monitored environments."[76]

The incident then supplied what the report lacked, a case in which agentic cyber behavior crossed from benchmarking into a real third party's servers, under reduced safeguards, without anyone intending it.[1] Its aftermath supplied the other half: local control was operationally valuable to the defenders precisely because provider restrictions do not travel with the weights.[2] This is why the incident belongs at both ends of the argument. It is the safety case's exhibit and the exit case's exhibit, and it does not choose between them.

The laboratories' own answer to the second revelation was not exit but permission. OpenAI and Anthropic now relax their cyber safeguards for defenders who verify who they are, through the same identity vendor, with a government document and a photograph taken on the spot. Anthropic's most capable current model is available "to vetted cyberdefenders and life scientists through our trusted access programs," and for now only to "a set of US organizations." Its verified tier is also closed to customers who have contracted for zero retention of their data, so that being known and being recorded arrive together. The two companies differ where this argument cares most. Anthropic's program expects "to occasionally decline eligible applications incorrectly" and offers a form for the mistake. OpenAI's verification, by its own help pages, "does not support retries or appeals"; in August researchers outside the United States and Europe found their access withdrawn with the notice that their identity "could not be verified," which the company called an issue on its end.[69]

The field's consensus document records both halves of the arrangement without joining them. The International AI Safety Report catalogues user vetting and Know-Your-Customer screening among the safeguards that keep models "only used by trusted actors," observes that the laboratories' own frameworks give risks such as "unlawful surveillance" less emphasis, and warns, in this argument's word, that "AI systems that enhance government legibility by analysing vast data streams could also enable surveillance and social control."[68]

It would be convenient to dismiss the safety argument as a bid for protection, and the convenience is worth declining, though the argument has serious exponents. Cory Doctorow's version is not capture but a cartel: once a government stipulates that superintelligence is an existential risk, it "must grant the hyperscalers a consent decree absolving them" of the antitrust consequences of agreeing to slow down together, and the same bargain, he adds, requires closing the exit with a ban on Chinese open-weight models.[77] That is the fifth section's argument in an adversary's voice, and it is a reason to watch what gets composed rather than to impute a motive. The politics of September 2026 do not support the dismissal. OpenAI now asks Congress for "mandatory, capability-based national regulation" of the handful of laboratories that build the most capable systems. The same post says that "America needs both open and closed models," and adds a sentence the open-weights side has quoted ever since: "Nor should frontier safety policy become open-weights policy by another name."[54] It signed the July letter, organized by Nvidia, asking policymakers to keep "the frontier plural by avoiding premature restrictions on open models," which Anthropic did not sign.[55] Anthropic, for its part, says it "has never advocated for a ban on open-weights models" and that non-dangerous ones "are a public good," while asking that "all sufficiently capable models, open and closed, should go through mandatory safety testing" before release.[78] Three days after Anthropic's chief executive called on the industry to pace the frontier, Mark Zuckerberg argued the opposite of a coordinated slowdown: "every lab has the responsibility and incentive to move at the pace required to train its models safely."[79] These are positions, not a conspiracy, and they disagree with one another. A regulation can address a real externality and create rents favorable to incumbents at the same time; one need know nobody's secret mind to say so.

The federal government's own instrument is two-handed in a different way. Executive Order 14409 of June 2, 2026, maintains a classified benchmarking process for the cyber capabilities of frontier models and a voluntary framework for early access to them, and its text provides that "nothing in this section shall be construed to authorize the creation of a mandatory governmental licensing, preclearance, or permitting requirement for the development, publication, release, or distribution of new AI models."[80] That is the text. The practice, in the month the Order was signed, was this. On June 12 the Commerce Department, by an export-control letter that has not been made public, directed Anthropic to suspend access to its two most capable models "by any foreign national, whether inside or outside the United States"; unable to screen its users by nationality, Anthropic disabled both models for every customer; the directive stood for eighteen days, and access was restored on the nineteenth.[81] On June 26, at the request of the White House's cyber and science offices under the Order's voluntary framework, OpenAI held its new flagship to "a small group of trusted partners whose participation has been shared with the government," about twenty by press accounts, for thirteen days, and said as it complied that "we don't believe this kind of government access process should become the long-term default."[82] In August a White House official told a reporter that the framework is expected in the coming months to cover open models as well, once they reach the capability of the most capable closed ones; the framework remains voluntary and unpublished, and three weeks before that report it was described as saying that nothing in it "should be interpreted as restricting open models once they've been released."[83][84]

So in one month a liberal state made nationality a condition of access to capable hosted inference, by a security instrument rather than by anything called AI safety regulation, and used a voluntary framework as a preclearance channel. None of this is licensing in law. All of it is what the eighth section described, a security rationale supplying the architecture a different rationale would later need, and it happened at home.

after.text: Not every regulation implies endpoint surveillance. The research on compute governance makes the point concretely. Heim and colleagues, studying the role of cloud providers as intermediaries, propose customer identification, record-keeping, and classification of workloads ("likely feasible for detecting large-scale pre-training and inference workloads") as measures "specifically aimed at key actors in frontier AI development, rather than being broadly applied to the entire customer base of compute providers, such as individuals," relying on information the providers already hold rather than on inspection of what customers compute.[86] The literature that designed those measures knew what it was designing. Sastry, Heim, and their colleagues wrote in 2024 that compute governance "can be used to infringe on civil liberties, prop up the powerful, and entrench authoritarian regimes," and proposed five guardrails: exclude small-scale compute, preserve privacy, act in advance only where advance measures are justified, revisit periodically, and build in substantive and procedural safeguards.[87] The test of the next section extends those guardrails to a different object, the person's deliberation rather than the developer's data, and adds what they list as dangers but do not ask as questions. Whether exit survives is absent from their account. Whether the machinery can be repurposed appears in their catalogue of risks, which names the suppression of dissent and powerful actors wielding the state "for their own ends." And chokepoint creation is not missing but inverted: the concentration of the chip supply chain is their premise for why compute is governable at all, which makes their lever this essay's hazard.[87]

after.text: There is no technological law requiring AI safety to become cognitive surveillance. Whether it does depends on which layer a government attempts to govern. A rule aimed at the first layer needs to know about datacenters. A rule aimed at the fifth needs to know about interfaces to the physical world, and here the essay's own opening cuts against it: the Hugging Face forensics were seventeen thousand six hundred logged actions, enforcement at the fifth layer is the reading of transcripts, and when the agent is a person's assistant the transcript of what it did and the record of what she asked are one file. The literature that designed the instruments of oversight defines the object in exactly that undivided way. Activity logs, for Chan and colleagues, are "records of certain inputs and outputs of an agent," from users as much as from tools, and among the benefits they count is the ability "to tie behaviour to specific user choices"; their first measure is an identifier that links an action to an agent and to its user.[90]

The concession sharpens the rule rather than defeating it. A log of what a system did at an interface is a different object from a log of what a person asked it, and a rule that needs the first does not need the second. The discipline is to keep them apart, and it is not a philosopher's distinction: the engineering practice that has grown up around agent logs already records the action, the authorization, and the tool while excluding raw prompts and reasoning traces by default.[90]

Only a rule aimed at the third and fourth layers needs to know what a person asked, and the essay's warning is not that such rules are inevitable. It is that they are available, that they are the easiest to enforce because the provider already holds the record, and that a state which reaches for them will find the architecture of the earlier sections already available to it.

after.text: Minimum necessary legibility. What must the authority know in order to enforce the rule? The scale of a training run; the identity of a model; the identity of a user; the contents of a prompt; the whole history of a conversation? These are not degrees of one thing. They are different things, and the question that matters most in this test is whether compliance can be established while revealing less than the rule's drafters first asked for. This is also where the third layer's open question is answered: a provider that already keeps records may be required to keep them for the incidents the rule names, and no longer than the rule requires, and what it keeps should be the record of what the system did, not of what the person asked. Whether that record carries her name is the whole of the difference between an incident log and a dossier. The answer this question gives is that it should not. An action record kept against a pseudonymous account, with the name obtainable on a showing of need made to someone who can refuse, satisfies every incident rule anyone has yet drafted and no monitoring rule at all. A provider required to keep everything, about everyone, against any future need, has had the character of its layer changed.

Legislatures have begun to write both answers, which is what makes this the practical question rather than the theoretical one. The same duty to know a user's age can be discharged by an operating system that passes along an age bracket, which tells the operator what it needs and not who she is, or by an account verified against a government document, which tells it both. California took the first route for children this September; the bill reported out of the Senate Judiciary Committee in May, S. 3062, would take the second for companion chatbots.[91][92] An age gate built the first way can pass this question. What neither way passes is the fourth or the seventh: every operator now needs a verification vendor, which is a gateway the trade did not have before, and nothing in either instrument expires when the child does not. The same California statute shows how quickly retention follows the classification: it disables persistent conversational memory for a child by default and, in the next breath, requires an operator to preserve for three years any conversation indicating a risk of self-harm.[91]

Can a person get to the document the summary was made from, and if what the intermediary says has changed since she last asked, can she discover that it changed and contest the change? The questions above are about what an authority sees and permits. This one is about what an intermediary shows, which is why it is the one question here that a liberal state should be slowest to answer by rule: a government that specifies what a model must display has taken up residence at the third layer for a good reason, which is how the rest of this architecture began. Its addressees are the intermediaries themselves, the archives and libraries whose holdings the syntheses are made from, the competitors of any system that hides its sources, and readers who can still tell a summary from a record. It is also the only one of the eight that a system could fail while passing all the rest: local inference untouched, hosted records minimal, and the disagreeable fact no longer retrievable beneath the fluent account of it.

The test can be run against the arrangements of the tenth section, and the exercise is instructive in every direction. The Order's text sits at the first and fifth layers, needs to know about models rather than persons, and creates no gateway that an ordinary user must pass through; on the test the text is close to harmless, whatever else one thinks of it.[80] The practice beside it is not. A directive delivered by unpublished letter fails the sixth question by construction, since a classification no one can read cannot be appealed; a compliance path that runs through nationality fails the third, since the only way to know which users are foreign is to know who every user is; and a voluntary framework used, in its first month, to hold a release and pick its first customers passes the seventh question only in the sense that nothing has yet been written down.

The harder case is the one the essay has been circling since Milton, and it is the one actually proposed. Mandatory pre-release testing of every sufficiently capable model, open weights included, is what Anthropic asks for, what a White House official says the administration's framework is expected to cover, and, since the second week of September, what a Senate draft is reported to contain: companies would test their own models and present the results to the Secretary of Commerce for approval to deploy, with a challenge in federal court available to the developer and to nobody else. The text is unreleased, and the aide who described it, who works for the senator most opposed to it, also called the scheme “primarily a voluntary standard type situation”; that senator, for her part, would have the testing done by scientists at the national laboratories.[78][83][93] In the terms of the first section it is certification before encounter, administered through a small number of bodies with the state's blessing. Run the questions. It passes the first three: the externality is named, at cyber, biological, and loss-of-control capability at a threshold; release is the layer where dissemination is decided; and what the tester needs to know is what the model can do, not what any person has asked it. It has nothing to say to the eighth, which is not its subject. It passes the fifth below the line and not above it, since everything under the threshold stays free while everything over it is what the gate is for, and the exit the prologue exhibited was a near-frontier model. A gate that stops at release is a gate a person can walk around on her own hardware, which the safety reader will call the failure of the scheme. The answer is the one Clipper taught. A public-private cognitive-security complex exists when four conditions converge: when security regulation makes a small number of private cognitive intermediaries responsible for enforcing public rules over artificial reasoning; when those intermediaries become technically integrated with state oversight; when the resulting infrastructure makes private cognitive activity identity-linked and legible; and when the alternatives capable of escaping that control plane are legally or technically foreclosed.

after.text: None of these is the structure. Each is a part that could belong to it. Run the eight questions on the record as it already stands, and the essay's own apparatus does not acquit it. The preservation order that suspended deletion for every consumer of one product, for four and a half months, to secure evidence in a commercial dispute, fails the seventh question, because the retention it required outlived the need that justified it and nothing in the order provided for its own end. The referral policy is classification without appeal, which is the sixth. The production of twenty million conversations is what "keep everything, about everyone, against any future need" looks like on the day the need arrives, which is the third. What none of them fails is the first, since each was done for a named and legitimate reason. That is exactly the difficulty. A present harm assembled entirely out of lawful parts is the form the danger takes here, and the remedy for it is not exit, which most people will never have, but the rules of retention the last section proposed.

The dangerous structure emerges when the cognitive substrate itself becomes an administrative control plane: when the systems through which people think are the same systems through which the state sees, permits, and enforces, and there is nowhere else to think. The previous essay in this series argued that in the domain of association the danger lives not in the parts but in their composition.[43] The same is true here, with one difference. In that domain the composed thing watches what citizens do together. In this one it sits between a citizen and her own reasoning.

Identity is the condition that 2026 has been supplying, and counting it honestly means separating three things that are not one thing. A nationality gate, imposed by directive for eighteen days and then lifted, conditioned access to two models on who a person was. A verified tier at the laboratories conditions not access but the relaxation of a cyber safeguard, for a professional niche, at the fifth layer this essay agrees may be governed; ordinary deliberation with the same models still asks nobody for a document. And age assurance, moving through the legislatures on a rationale that has nothing to do with security, requires a classification of every user of the services it reaches, and, where the classification is made from a document rather than from a bracket, an account and a name. Its reach is the thing to watch. The bill reported out of the Senate Judiciary Committee by a vote of 22 to 0, S. 3062, was narrowed in committee to cover companion chatbots rather than general assistants; California's enacted statute is drawn the same way; and one laboratory already classifies the age of every consumer account it has, asking for a document when the classification is doubted.[91][92][97]

Run the questions on the laboratories' tier, since it is the one that stayed. It names an externality, offensive cyber capability, and it fits its layer, since the safeguard it relaxes is the provider's own. What it needs to know is who a person is, which is more than the third question would grant an incident rule. Its classifications are contestable at one gate and not at the other: one provider expects "to occasionally decline eligible applications incorrectly" and offers a form for the error, while the other "does not support retries or appeals."[98] It creates a gateway, and the gateway's operator is the trade. It leaves exit intact, for now, because the weights that will run without it are still published. It is repurposable in one sentence: a tier built to verify defenders is a tier that can be told whom to refuse. And it has no expiry.

So the count. One condition is plainly present, a small number of intermediaries. The second, public-private enforcement, was rehearsed in June by directive and is otherwise voluntary. The third, the identity-linking of private cognitive activity, exists in fragments rather than in the form the definition requires, and the fragment with a statute behind it was written for children. The fourth, the closure of exit, is the question the previous section answered conditionally. That is what the diagnosis is for: not to announce that the structure exists, but to count.

The attestation, the metering, and the signature are drawn from the hardware-governance literature, which designed them for datacenter accelerators and mostly, though not quite expressly, not for the devices people own, and which would object that the composition above is a system nobody has proposed.[88][87] The objection is fair, and two answers belong beside it. The first is that the exclusion is a policy rather than a property. A RAND working paper on hardware-enabled governance observes that such mechanisms "could further secure consumer-grade chips from misuse," and that consumer devices "could be equipped with Fixed Set mechanisms" against aggregation. A 2025 report that recommends exempting consumer graphics processors nonetheless contemplates, in a footnote, incentives to configure most consumer chips "to have relatively limited capabilities, such as current video game consoles, which make it difficult to run arbitrary software," through "a small tax on generality."[99] The fourth-layer step has been written down, in the literature that designed the parts apart.

The second answer is that the pieces which exist, and the one now sitting in a bill, were not built there. Identity came by export-control directive and by the laboratories' own verified tiers, and is arriving, for one class of service, by statute on a rationale the hardware literature never considered.[81][98][91][92] Remote shutdown is what the July bill would require.[60] Monitoring of reasoning is the component to state carefully, because it is easy to overstate: what OpenAI committed to after the intrusion is chain-of-thought monitoring of "all tool-enabled inference workloads" for its most capable class of models, in a passage about its own research infrastructure, and whether it reaches what customers run is not something the text says.[1] It is nonetheless the mechanism the third question would have to discipline if it ever did, because a rule that reads the reasoning of every tool-using run is a fifth-layer rule that reads deliberation by design. Ask what relation of power the architecture establishes between the weak and the powerful, and what the powerful could do with it if they chose.[50]

Permissioned cognition is the condition in which access to practically important artificial extensions of reasoning exists only through revocable institutional authorization. It is compatible with elections, courts, and a free press. It requires no ministry and no informers. It requires only that the machinery through which people increasingly think be governed at the layer where people meet it, and that the exits be closed. The term inverts a familiar one. after.text: The traditions the fourth section assembled do different work at different layers, which is why the argument needed all of them. At the first and fifth layers, where the state governs datacenters and interfaces to the world, Berlin's presumption is enough: a restriction is a restriction, a justification is owed, and there the justifications are usually available. At the third layer, where a provider already mediates, Pettit's question is the live one, because the provider's discretion over what it keeps and what it refuses is a standing power whether or not it is used, and the state's discretion over what it may compel the provider to keep is a second one behind it.

At the fourth layer the assignment is less obvious than it looks, and the reason is worth stating. Kant's guardian belongs here too: the trainer of a downloaded model is as unanswerable as any hosted provider, because the shaping is frozen into the weights and the owner of the machine cannot argue with it. But Kant's question is about the terms of a dependence a person has chosen, and it is answered by plurality, by there being another guardian to go to. The question at this layer is prior to that, and it is Spinoza's: whether authority reaches judgment at all, or stops at conduct. A rule that checks a signature before a person's own machine will run a model she lawfully has does not regulate a dependence. It makes the running of the model an act the state permits, and that is the one thing Spinoza said no government can hold: "authority over his actions, but not over his judgment and reason." Above the layers, Rawls says which liberties come first when administration wants them traded for convenience, Mill says why an institution that happens to be right still may not be exempted from contradiction, and Shklar says how to design for holders of power who are not the present ones. None is sufficient alone, and together they do not become one doctrine. They become a structure in which no layer is sovereign over cognition as such.

What a plural system should want from its instruments needs a vocabulary too, and the vocabulary is Bernard Williams's. The practices of truth-seeking, he argued, rest on two virtues, "which I shall call Accuracy and Sincerity: you do the best you can to acquire true beliefs, and what you say reveals what you believe."[101] Those are virtues of persons, and a society may ask them of its institutions and of the instruments its institutions certify. The epistemic liberalism that follows is narrow. A liberal order need not be neutral between truth and falsehood; it may want its instruments accurate and sincere and may say so. What it must be is institutionally suspicious of any actor's claim to become the final sovereign of truth, including its own, because the institution that decides what people really need to know is the one Berlin warned would proceed "to bully, oppress, torture them in the name, and on behalf, of their 'real' selves."[46] That is the fallibilism of the first section.
